claim: One child per minute still dies of malaria globally.
source: One child per minute still dies of malaria globally (WHO, 2015a)
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2015a report

claim: Dengue infects an estimated four hundred million individuals per year.
source: dengue infects an estimated four hundred million individuals per year (Bhatt et al., 2013; Murray et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhatt et al., 2013 and Murray et al., 2013

claim: Evolution persistently undermines vector control programs through insecticide resistance.
source: Evolution persistently undermines vector control programs through insecticide resistance.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about insecticide resistance evolution

claim: Both theory and experience point to the inevitability of resistance to conventional insecticides.
source: both theory and experience pointing to the inevitability of resistance to conventional insecticides (Brogdon and McAllister, 1998; Hemingway et al., 2002; Nauen, 2007; Asidi et al., 2012; Hemingway and Ranson, 2000; Ndiath et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to scientific literature

claim: Mosquito populations have considerable potential to evolve.
source: It is clear that mosquito populations have considerable potential to evolve
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about mosquito evolution

claim: DDT has both high toxicity and high spatial repellence in the absence of resistance.
source: In the absence of resistance, DDT, the most effective chemical used to date for the control of malaria vectors, has both high toxicity and high spatial repellence (Kennedy, 1947; Grieco et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kennedy, 1947 and Grieco et al., 2007

claim: Malaria vectors targeted by public health campaigns typically feed indoors between dusk and dawn.
source: The malaria vectors targeted by public health campaigns using bednets and indoor residual spraying of insecticides (IRS) typically feed indoors between dusk and dawn.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about malaria vector behavior

claim: Syafruddin et al. conducted a proof-of-concept double-blind placebo-controlled field trial using spatial repellents disbursed from burning coils that recorded an approximately 50% reduction in malaria infections in repellent-protected properties.
source: Syafruddin et al. have conducted a proof-of-concept double-blind placebo-controlled field trial using spatial repellents disbursed from burning coils. This trial recorded an approximately 50% reduction in malaria infections in repellent-protected properties (Syafruddin et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Syafruddin et al., 2014 field trial

claim: Finding suitable new repellent substances is a particularly challenging task.
source: the limited choice and efficacy of currently available compounds suitable for this purpose suggests that finding suitable new repellent substances is a particularly challenging task
evidence: Inferred from the limited availability of effective repellents

claim: DDT carries a reputational burden from its historic overuse such that environmental concerns make its continued use problematic and its continued availability uncertain.
source: DDT itself carries a reputational burden from its historic overuse, such that environmental concerns make its continued use problematic and its continued availability uncertain.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about DDT's environmental concerns

claim: Combining a spatial repellent with a low-contact-repellence high-toxicity insecticide can lead to a 'double-dip' system of disease control.
source: we propose a combination of a spatial repellent, which deters mosquitoes from entering buildings, with a low-contact-repellence high-toxicity insecticide, which kills those which do enter, leading to a 'double-dip' system of disease control
evidence: This is the main theoretical proposal of the manuscript

claim: If the fitness cost of being deflected is less than the fitness cost of being susceptible to the insecticide, there is potential for selection to favour an increase in the proportion of deflected individuals in the treated population.
source: Provided that, in a given context, the fitness cost of being deflected is less than the fitness cost of being susceptible to the insecticide, there is potential for selection to favour an increase in the proportion of deflected individuals in the treated population.
evidence: Based on logical inference from evolutionary principles

claim: The model assumes physiological insecticide resistance is controlled by a single locus bi-allelic autosomal gene, with the resistance allele being completely dominant to the susceptibility allele.
source: (1) Physiological insecticide resistance is controlled by a single locus bi-allelic autosomal gene, with the resistance allele being completely dominant to the susceptibility allele.
evidence: This is a stated model assumption

claim: The model assumes deflection by a given spatial repellent is controlled by a single locus bi-allelic autosomal gene, with the deflection allele being completely dominant to the non-deflection allele.
source: (2) Deflection by a given spatial repellent is controlled by a single locus bi-allelic autosomal gene, with the deflection allele being completely dominant to the non-deflection allele.
evidence: This is a stated model assumption

claim: There are examples of single-locus insecticide-resistance genes, including the knockdown resistance (kdr) alleles that provide resistance to DDT and pyrethroids.
source: there are examples of single-locus insecticide-resistance genes, including the knockdown resistance (kdr) alleles that provide resistance to DDT and pyrethroids (Ndiath et al., 2012; Chandre et al., 2000; Jones et al., 2012; Dabiré et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to scientific literature

claim: For some combinations of fitness values and initial allele proportions, the deflection allele spreads rapidly to near-fixation and remains consistently at that level for at least 300 cycles.
source: As illustrated in Figure 1, for some combinations of fitness values and initial allele proportions, the deflection allele spreads rapidly to near-fixation, and remains consistently at that level for at least 300 cycles (panels labelled 'a')
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 1

claim: In some cases, the deflection allele spreads initially but falls away within 300 cycles as the resistance allele spreads.
source: In other cases, the deflection allele spreads initially, but falls away within 300 cycles as the resistance allele spreads (panels labelled 'b')
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 1

claim: In some cases the deflection allele shows only minimal spread before being lost as resistance spreads.
source: in some cases the deflection allele shows only minimal spread before being lost as resistance spreads (panels labelled 'c')
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 1

claim: Swapping the insecticide for an alternative whilst the deflection allele is close to its peak prevalence can allow a 'ratchet' effect, whereby the deflection allele is able to spread and reach sustained high levels.
source: For cases like that in 'b', where deflection spreads initially but then falls away, we considered the outcome if the insecticide used is swapped for an alternative, for which resistance alleles are still relatively rare, whilst the deflection allele is close to its peak prevalence. In some cases this allows a 'ratchet' effect, whereby the deflection allele is able to spread and reach sustained high levels.
evidence: Based on model results and logical inference

claim: The fitness values for all phenotypes and the initial prevalence of deflection and resistance alleles all affect the potential for deflection alleles to spread and be maintained in the population.
source: A comparison of panels (i) to (iv) in Figure 2 shows that the fitness values for all phenotypes, and the initial prevalence of deflection and resistance alleles all affect the potential for deflection alleles to spread and be maintained in the population
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 2

claim: If a cost of resistance affects resistant deflected phenotypes, this serves to increase the range of deflection and resistance fitness combinations for which deflection alleles can spread and be maintained.
source: From comparison of Figure 2 panel (i) and Figure 3, it can be seen that if a cost of resistance affects resistant deflected phenotypes this serves to increase the range of deflection and resistance fitness combinations for which deflection alleles can spread and be maintained.
evidence: Supported by comparison of model results in Figures 2 and 3

claim: When assuming some reduction in transmission for deflected mosquitoes, the ESR offers an initial reduction in infectious bites very similar to that achieved initially with insecticide alone, with the benefit maintained or improved over the long term.
source: When assuming some reduction in transmission for deflected mosquitoes (lines with slash, circle and triangular markers), this trade-off between immediate and long-term benefits is reduced, with the ESR offering an initial reduction in infectious bites very similar to that achieved initially with insecticide alone, with the benefit again maintained or improved over the long term.
evidence: Supported by model results shown in Figure 4

claim: DDT may have maintained efficacy as a transmission-reduction agent through its action as an effective spatial repellent even when resistance to its toxic effects was widely observed.
source: By the time of its withdrawal,resistance to the toxic effects of DDT was already widely observed, but there is empirical evidence to suggest that it may nonetheless have maintained efficacy as a transmission-reduction agent through its action as an effective spatial repellent (Roberts et al., 2000; Roberts and Alecrim, 1991)
evidence: Supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2000 and Roberts and Alecrim, 1991

claim: Many substances investigated because of their repellent properties are also toxic on contact with target species.
source: In fact, many substances investigated because of their repellent properties are also toxic on contact with target species. These include DEET, probably the most effective and well-known of the available repellents, as well as many of the naturally repellent plant-based volatiles currently in use or under investigation for personal protection (Xue et al., 2003; Licciardi et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citations to Xue et al., 2003 and Licciardi et al., 2006

claim: Carbosulfan, the most toxic of three public-health insecticides, demonstrated high spatial repellence in a population of susceptible mosquitoes but not in a resistant population.
source: A comparison of the behavioural and insecticidal effects of three public-health insecticides provides more direct evidence of toxicity giving rise to repellency. The most toxic of the three, carbosulfan, also demonstrated high spatial repellence in a population of susceptible mosquitoes but not in a resistant population (Malima et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Malima et al., 2009

claim: Control programs should target high coverage with high-efficacy insecticides to minimize the fitness of non-deflected susceptibles.
source: The potential for establishing an ESR is maximized by lower fitness values for susceptibles and by higher fitness values for deflected phenotypes, indicating that control programs should target high coverage with high-efficacy insecticides to minimize the fitness of non-deflected susceptibles.
evidence: Based on logical inference from model results

claim: All treated properties should ideally be treated with both an insecticide and ESR, rather than with either alone, in order to maximize selection for deflection and to minimize selection for physiological resistance.
source: Critically, all treated properties should ideally be treated with both an insecticide and ESR, rather than with either alone, in order to maximize selection for deflection and to minimize selection for physiological resistance.
evidence: Based on logical inference from model results and evolutionary principles

claim: Fungal biopesticides being developed for vector control potentially offer an ideal partnership with a spatial repellency treatment as they appear to have no contact repellency and have inherent resistance management benefits.
source: Furthermore fungal biopesticides being developed for vector control potentially offer an ideal partnership with a spatial repellency treatment, whether DDT or a novel chemical, as they appear to have no contact repellency and have inherent resistance management benefits (Thomas and Read, 2007; Mnyone et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Thomas and Read, 2007 and Mnyone et al., 2010

claim: The excito-repellent properties of some pyrethroid insecticides currently used on long-lasting insecticide-treated nets reduce the mortality they generate by pushing vectors away before they acquire a lethal dose.
source: The excito-repellent properties of some of the pyrethroid insecticides currently used on long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) reduce the mortality they generate by pushing vectors away before they acquire a lethal dose (Grieco et al., 2007; Tananchai et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Grieco et al., 2007 and Tananchai et al., 2012

claim: Ndiath et al. found no sporozooites in a population of insecticide-susceptible An. gambiae pushed to outdoor feeding by the deployment of LLINs in Dielmo, whilst transmission continued at a high level in an indoor-feeding resistant population.
source: Ndiath et al. (Ndiath et al., 2014) found no sporozooites in a population of insecticide-susceptible An. gambiae pushed to outdoor feeding by the deployment of LLINs in Dielmo, whilst transmission continued at a high level in an indoor-feeding resistant population (Ndiath et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ndiath et al., 2014

claim: For vectors that preferentially feed indoors, there is an expected fitness cost to a switch to outdoor feeding.
source: For vectors that preferentially feed indoors, there is an expected fitness cost to a switch to outdoor feeding.
evidence: Based on logical inference from evolutionary principles

claim: The transition to outdoor feeding will be at least partly reversible if the response to an ESR ceases when the ESR is withdrawn.
source: This means that, should outdoor feeding prove undesirable at some point, the transition to outdoor feeding will be at least partly reversible since, unlike direct responses to an insecticide or to entering buildings, the response to an ESR will cease to affect vector behaviour if the ESR is withdrawn.
evidence: Based on logical inference about behavioral responses

claim: ESR does not require the withdrawal or reduction of existing control measures in order to be effective.
source: As well as being reversible in its effects, unlike many resistance-management strategies, ESR does not require the withdrawal or reduction of existing control measures in order to be effective.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the proposed mechanism

claim: Gould suggested in 1984 that some insect populations might be expected to evolve behavioural avoidance of agricultural insecticides which were not originally repellent to them.
source: it is interesting to note that in the early 1980s Gould (1984) suggested that some insect populations might be expected to evolve behavioural avoidance of agricultural insecticides which were not originally repellent to them
evidence: Supported by citation to Gould, 1984

claim: Gould suggested that in many situations, physiological resistance would evolve more slowly to insecticide formulations with high repellency than to non-repellent formulations.
source: in many situations, physiological resistance would evolve more slowly to insecticide formulations with high repellency than to non-repellent formulations
evidence: Supported by citation to Gould, 1984
